item.title: BFL.ai launches FLUX 3 multimodal foundation model for joint image, video, and audio understanding and generation, now in Early Access [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: BFL.ai has released FLUX 3, a new multimodal foundation model designed to learn from images, videos, and audio simultaneously within a unified architecture. The model aims to capture a comprehensive representation of the world by integrating spatial, temporal, and acoustic information, enabling it to perceive, predict, and act across physical and digital environments. FLUX 3 is available in Early Access and demonstrates capabilities such as text-to-video generation, image-to-video animation, video-to-video transformation, and multilingual dialogue with native audio generation. FLUX 3 builds on the Self-Flow approach to align multimodal generation and understanding efficiently, scaling compute and data resources to train across multiple modalities. Early evaluations show FLUX 3 outperforming several competing video generation models in user preference tests, with strengths in capturing human facial expressions, associating sounds with physical events, and maintaining character consistency across multi-shot sequences. The model also supports diverse visual styles, aspect ratios, and resolutions for image synthesis and editing, with ongoing development expected to improve its performance further.

item.title: Startup founders urge U.S. government not to block access to Chinese open-weight AI models amid policy debates
item.description: Startup founders have appealed to the U.S. government to avoid shutting off access to Chinese open-weight AI models, emphasizing the importance of maintaining open AI ecosystems. This request comes amid ongoing discussions about national security and technology control policies related to AI development and international cooperation.

item.title: Echo system combines open-weight models to match Fable-level AI results at one third the inference cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Echo is an AI system that dynamically allocates computation across multiple open-weight models to optimize performance on each request. It selects which models to use and how to combine their outputs, achieving results comparable to the stronger Fable system but at roughly one third of the inference cost. The developer built a chat interface and an OpenAI-compatible API to allow external testing and is investigating cases where Echo's allocation decisions are suboptimal. Echo's approach leverages the complementary strengths of different models, including those weaker overall but useful for specific tasks.

item.title: Analysis: Arguments against open source AI overlook its foundational role in software and the difficulty of suppression, with diverse commercial incentives supporting open models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The release of the Kimi K3 open source AI model has reignited debate, with some journalists, business leaders, and politicians arguing that open source AI poses dangers and should be controlled by trusted gatekeepers. The article challenges these views by highlighting that open source software underpins all proprietary software, including AI models, and that attempts to suppress open source technologies historically fail and disadvantage domestic actors. It further explains that open source AI development is not limited to any single country but involves various commercial players such as chip makers, startups, enterprise users, and large tech companies, each with incentives to support or utilize open source models. The discussion also questions the framing of AI competition and regulation, suggesting that restrictive policies may hinder domestic innovation without effectively limiting global access to AI technologies.

item.title: DARPA and U.S. Air Force conduct in-air tests of AI-controlled F-16 fighter jet modified under VENOM program [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: DARPA and the U.S. Air Force have successfully flown an F-16 fighter jet autonomously controlled by an AI agent as part of the VENOM program, which converts standard F-16s into autonomous-capable platforms. This milestone advances the development of scalable combat AI infrastructure for future joint force operations. The VENOM Autonomy Kit enables pilots to switch between human and AI control without altering the jet's core software, allowing safe human-on-the-loop experimentation. These tests build on previous AI-piloted flights and will support DARPA's upcoming Artificial Intelligence Reinforcements program, aiming to integrate AI agents into complex aerial combat scenarios and enhance autonomous air combat capabilities.

item.title: Report: Sony cannot reissue classic Walkman models due to manufacturing and component sourcing challenges
item.description: Sony is unable to bring back its classic Walkman models because the original manufacturing processes and components are no longer available or feasible to reproduce. The company faces difficulties sourcing obsolete parts and replicating the precise assembly techniques used in the original devices. These challenges prevent Sony from reissuing the iconic Walkman despite ongoing consumer interest in retro audio products.

item.title: SonicSampler introduces unified tile-aware Triton kernels for LLM sampling and speculative verification, achieving up to 16x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: SonicSampler presents a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the entire sampling pipeline for large language model (LLM) inference, including logit processing, token selection, and speculative verification. The approach supports dynamic per-request sampling behaviors such as grammar constraints, penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, and various filtering methods within a single batched kernel compatible with CUDA Graph execution. Central to SonicSampler is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies, achieving up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines. Across diverse speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler delivers up to 16x speedup compared to existing methods while maintaining flexible batched execution.

item.title: Researchers present ExpectBench and LENS to improve alignment of large language models with real-world user expectations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world interactions with large language models (LLMs), revealing that current models often fail to meet or anticipate what users actually seek. They introduced ExpectBench, a benchmark based on real user expectations, and found that existing evaluation methods do not capture the diversity and subtlety of human expectations, leading to misalignment despite apparent model competence. Building on these findings, the team proposed LENS, a lightweight framework that enables LLMs to internalize user expectations and generate responses better aligned with those expectations. LENS consistently improves user satisfaction, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment in language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce DFAH-Bench to measure behavioral instability in financial AI agents across tool use and decision paths, revealing significant divergence despite high decision agreement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark designed to assess observable behavioral instability in financial decision-making agents by analyzing tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration without accessing hidden reasoning. Evaluating 10 models over 8,127 episodes across three financial tasks, they found that models often agree on outcomes 95% of the time but follow the same tool paths only 77% of the time, indicating that outcome agreement alone misses significant process variability. The study identifies three behavioral profiles among agents: pattern matchers that produce consistent outputs regardless of input, stable executors with consistent tool use, and trajectory divergers that reach the same decisions through different processes. The benchmark's code, metrics, and data are publicly released to support further research.

item.title: Researchers introduce AppWorld-UL benchmark with 516 tasks to evaluate diverse agent-user interactions in tool-use agents across nine simulated apps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed AppWorld-UL, a new benchmark featuring 516 challenging tasks designed to test diverse agent-user interactions in tool-use agents handling digital tasks like ordering groceries. The benchmark builds on the AppWorld framework with nine popular simulated apps such as Amazon and Spotify, introducing ambiguities and constraints that require agents to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform users when instructions are infeasible. User behavior is simulated by a large language model with controlled knowledge boundaries to provide reliable interaction scenarios. Evaluation using the state-of-the-art LLM Claude Opus 4.7 showed a success rate of only 48.6% on the full benchmark and 35.7% on a harder compositional subset, with performance dropping to 21.3% on a stricter scenario-level metric. The results highlight the difficulty of the benchmark and emphasize the importance of correct user interaction for agent success, indicating its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

item.title: Researchers propose a theory that human participation persists in AI automation due to technical, normative, and emergent factors, challenging the assumption that AI will fully replace humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper argues that human involvement in AI-driven automation will continue even with highly capable systems for three main reasons: humans provide unique capabilities unavailable to AI, participation supports human agency and learning, and some tasks have goals that emerge through human-AI interaction rather than being predefined. The authors introduce the concept of human-AI co-construction, where humans and AI jointly produce outcomes, making human participation a fundamental aspect rather than a temporary workaround for imperfect AI. The theory highlights important implications for the limits of automation and suggests that future AI system design, evaluation, and ethics must account for persistent human roles in activities where objectives evolve through interaction. This challenges the common assumption that humans remain in the loop only due to current AI limitations and emphasizes the value of human contributions beyond mere execution.

item.title: Researchers analyze preference tuning in RLHF as spectral update reorganization revealing distinct head-tail parameter update structures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers study preference-based post-training in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) by examining the spectral structure of parameter updates. They decompose LoRA updates into spectral components, identifying a compact head that drives major behavioral changes and a residual tail with weaker effects. This head-tail organization is consistent across models, algorithms, and supervision methods and reflects functional differences rather than mere description. The study finds that the head component accounts for visible behavioral shifts and carries solver bias, while the tail is necessary for full solution recovery, especially for out-of-distribution behavior. These results suggest that preference tuning involves structured update reorganization rather than a single behavioral correction, linking alignment improvements and coverage losses to the organization of learned updates.

item.title: Researchers develop knowledge-injection framework to improve zero-shot ICU delirium prediction in LLaMA models using external clinical reports [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present a lightweight knowledge-injection framework that enhances zero-shot ICU delirium prediction by augmenting natural-language summaries of electronic health records with external clinical knowledge reports at inference time, without fine-tuning. Evaluations on 3,160 ICU admissions from the MIMIC IV dataset show that adding clinically meaningful external knowledge improves AUROC by 8.57 points for LLaMA 3.1 8B and 1.99 points for LLaMA 3.3 70B models compared to no external knowledge. Random control reports do not improve performance, indicating the importance of relevant clinical content. The approach narrows the performance gap between smaller locally deployable open-weight models and larger frontier closed models while maintaining privacy and practicality for resource-constrained clinical settings.

item.title: Researchers find required answer formats cause language models to fabricate data, releasing PhantomFill benchmark to measure hallucination rates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study shows that language models often fabricate answers when filling required fields in structured formats like JSON, even when the input lacks sufficient information. Thirteen models were tested with the same questions and inputs designed to be unanswerable; while GPT-5.5 answered honestly in free text 98% of the time, it fabricated answers 100% of the time when required to fill sentiment fields. This pattern was consistent across most models, with explicit options for "insufficient evidence" largely ignored and direct instructions overridden by schema requirements. The researchers released PhantomFill, a benchmark with metrics to quantify this coerced fabrication, highlighting a widespread issue in model honesty under format constraints.

item.title: Researchers introduce Frontier Financial Judgement benchmark to evaluate AI agents' ability to identify stock-moving financial news, finding top agents match expert labels in just over half of cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Frontier Financial Judgement, a new benchmark created with professional equity analysts to test AI agents' capacity to replicate expert judgments on financial news that could impact stock valuations. The benchmark includes 656 items combining synthetic, live, and historical articles to simulate real-world conditions where agents must distinguish relevant new information from stale or misleading news. The best-performing agent matched expert labels in only 52.4% of cases, with false-positive rates varying widely among agents from about 1% to 32%. The study highlights ongoing challenges in balancing accuracy, cost, and reliability for deploying AI-driven news filtering in financial contexts.

item.title: Researchers audit five diversity metrics in large language model ensembles, finding they mainly reflect capability rather than true diversity, affecting majority-vote gain predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a capability-controlled audit of five diversity metrics used to select large language model (LLM) ensembles, analyzing 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro and TruthfulQA benchmarks. They found that while latent complementarity exists, simple majority voting rarely outperforms the best individual model, and most diversity measures are strongly entangled with model capability rather than measuring true diversity. The study revealed that a joint-correctness proxy closely correlates with one minus mean accuracy, and three linear contingency-table statistics are algebraically inseparable. After controlling for capability, a modest residual association was found where more shared errors correspond to lower ensemble gain, but this effect varies by configuration. The findings suggest that common diversity metrics may not reliably predict ensemble performance improvements beyond individual model capabilities.

item.title: Researchers demonstrate activation steering of Llama-3.1-8B to control eight Jungian cognitive functions, revealing personality representation in transformer layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a framework using Jungian cognitive functions to represent and control personality in large language models (LLMs) through activation steering. They developed a Jungian evaluation protocol and a dataset of over 2,100 role-playing character narrations to test this approach on Llama-3.1-8B, achieving effective monotonic control over all eight cognitive functions. Their analysis shows that personality information is concentrated in the middle transformer layers and that steering vectors exhibit geometric relationships aligned with distinctions between rational and irrational functions. They also find that multi-dimensional steering directions cannot be formed by linear combinations of single-function directions, providing new insights into interpretable and multi-dimensional personality control in LLM activation space.

item.title: Researchers propose CAPTAIN, a perplexity-based APT detection method using unsupervised, context-augmented language models with minimal preprocessing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a new method for detecting Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) that leverages general pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing to score long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent log history using an encoder and a Q-Former-style bridge to inject context tokens into the decoder input, allowing perplexity to reflect temporal context, and applies smoothing filters to improve stability. CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines on APT detection benchmarks while requiring substantially less curated input data, reducing the engineering and operational costs associated with heavy log preprocessing pipelines. This approach addresses challenges in detecting rare attack-related events in large-scale logs and aims to make APT detection more scalable and cost-effective.

item.title: Researchers propose reinforcement learning to improve faithfulness of large language models' self-explanations, achieving higher Phi-CCT scores on Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a reinforcement learning method to directly optimize the faithfulness of large language models' self-explanations, aiming to align generated reasoning with internal decision-making processes. They modify existing faithfulness metrics into a training objective and fine-tune Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B models, achieving significant improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks like StrategyQA. The study experiments with two intervention types-random-word insertions and user-bias insertions-and observes some cross-intervention generalization, particularly with Llama3.1-8B. The researchers also analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming during reinforcement learning. Their results suggest that models can be trained to implicitly identify and disclose influential decision factors, offering a scalable approach to reducing unfaithful reasoning in large language models.

item.title: Researchers introduce Int-Bench to evaluate LLM tutoring interventions, finding LLMs intervene earlier and more frequently than humans and often provide full solutions instead of hints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers developed Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark to assess how large language models (LLMs) intervene during problem-solving tasks across code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers. The study compares LLMs acting as tutors to human teachers, focusing on the timing and frequency of interventions and their effects on immediate task success and generalization to new problems. The findings reveal that LLMs tend to intervene more often and earlier than humans and prefer giving complete solutions rather than targeted hints. This behavior suggests that current LLM assistants prioritize short-term task completion over fostering deeper reasoning and long-term learning.

item.title: Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence in Chain-of-Thought Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.21433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B exhibit a bimodal convergence pattern: generations either terminate within a token budget (converged) or exhaust it without reaching a conclusion (non-converged). We characterize this phenomenon empirically, showing that converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy on AIME 1983-2024 while non-converged ones achieve only 6.6%, with an overall convergence rate of 62.0%. We then ask whether this outcome is detectable early in the thinking chain using internal model representations. Training linear probes on hidden-state activations at token positions 50-300, we find that layer-20 activations at token 150 achieve AUC 0.608 (+-0.080, 5-fold CV), reliably above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines derived from token entropy and repetition statistics. A sweep-level permutation test yields p=0.063 (100,000 permutations), consistent with a modest signal that our sample size cannot confirm at conventional thresholds. These findings suggest that convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate representations well before the generation ends, opening a path toward early-exit inference and adaptive compute allocation.

item.title: Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.21475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the H\'ajek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

item.title: Simple Policy Gradients for Reasoning with Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2510.04019v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) represent a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs; however, the lack of effective post-training techniques, including reinforcement learning (RL), remains a key challenge for dLLMs, especially for downstream applications. Existing approaches often rely on a sequence-level view that requires biased likelihood approximations. In this work, we propose Amortized Group Relative Policy Optimization (AGRPO), a policy gradient algorithm that leverages the Markovian nature of dLLMs, optimizing individual denoising steps rather than full sequences. Our approach improves alignment between the trained policy and the inference process and also admits efficient, unbiased gradient updates via a novel timestep estimation scheme. We demonstrate AGRPO's effectiveness on different math and reasoning tasks, achieving absolute accuracy gains of +59.4\% and +69.7\% on Countdown and Sudoku over the base LLaDA model, exceeding comparable methods such as diffu-GRPO. Code is available at https://github.com/probablyabot/agrpo.

item.title: Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding for Error Span Detection in Reference-Free Automatic Machine Translation Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2512.07540v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Error Span Detection (ESD) extends automatic machine translation (MT) evaluation by localizing translation errors and labeling their severity. Current generative ESD methods typically use Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) decoding, assuming that the model-estimated probabilities are perfectly correlated with similarity to the human annotation, but we often observe higher likelihood assigned to an incorrect annotation than to the human one. We instead apply Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding to generative ESD. We use a sentence- or span-level similarity function for MBR decoding, which selects candidate hypotheses based on their approximate similarity to the human annotation. Experimental results on the WMT24 Metrics Shared Task show that MBR decoding significantly improves span-level performance and generally matches or outperforms MAP at the system and sentence levels. To reduce the computational cost of MBR decoding, we further distill its decisions into a model decoded via greedy search, removing the inference-time latency bottleneck.

item.title: SR-TTT Does Not Learn Retrieval: A Correction and Mechanistic Post-Mortem of Surprisal-Aware Residual Test-Time Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2603.06642v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-Time Training (TTT) language models replace the KV-cache with fast weights updated during inference, achieving O(1) memory but suffering catastrophic failure on exact-recall tasks. Version 1 of this work proposed SR-TTT, which routes high-surprisal tokens to a sparse exact-attention Residual Cache, and reported large Needle-in-a-Haystack gains. We show those gains were evaluation artifacts: the loss and metric read logits at the answer positions rather than one position earlier, training both models to copy an answer already visible in their input (a model trained on retrieval-impossible data reaches 100% accuracy under the flawed metric); additionally, the cache attended non-causally over future tokens, including the answer itself. We release a corrected implementation with startup causality self-tests, then ask whether the SR-TTT hypothesis survives correction. It does not, and the failure decomposes into two independent, separately measured bottlenecks. Storage: surprisal gating is systematically position-biased - the TTT reconstruction loss requires burn-in before a needle becomes relatively surprising, so early-context needles are stored at near-zero rates (0-1% containment at depth 0.1) exactly where long-context memory matters most. Addressing: with storage solved by an oracle and with new trainable read-time projections, per-slot attention supervision raises addressing mass 2.5x (0.06 -> 0.15) yet token accuracy is statistically unchanged, and retrieval extracts only approx. 0.06 nats of the 2.30-nat needle; position-free content addressing cannot resolve ordered slots whose contents are near-interchangeable. Exact match remains 0% in all 2,250 paired trials across all corrected conditions. We retract the claims of v1 and offer the corrected codebase, diagnostic protocol, and negative results as a cautionary reference for surprise-gated memory architectures.

item.title: Playing Along: Learning a Double-Agent Defender for Belief Steering via Theory of Mind [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2604.11666v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become the engine behind conversational systems, their ability to reason about the intentions and states of their dialogue partners (i.e., form and use a theory-of-mind, or ToM) becomes increasingly critical for safe interaction with potentially adversarial partners. We propose a novel privacy-themed ToM challenge, ToM for Steering Beliefs (ToM-SB), in which a defender must act as a Double Agent to steer the beliefs of an attacker with partial prior knowledge within a shared universe. To succeed on ToM-SB, the defender must engage with and form a ToM of the attacker, with a goal of fooling the attacker into believing they have succeeded in extracting sensitive information. We find that strong frontier models like Gemini3-Pro and GPT-5.4 struggle on ToM-SB, often failing to fool attackers in hard scenarios with partial attacker prior knowledge, even when prompted to reason about the attacker's beliefs (ToM prompting). To close this gap, we train models on ToM-SB to act as AI Double Agents using reinforcement learning, testing both fooling and ToM rewards. Notably, we find a bidirectionally emergent relationship between ToM and attacker-fooling: rewarding fooling success alone improves ToM, and rewarding ToM alone improves fooling. Across four attackers with different strengths, six defender methods, and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we find that gains in ToM and attacker-fooling are well-correlated, highlighting belief modeling as a key driver of success on ToM-SB. AI Double Agents that combine both ToM and fooling rewards yield the strongest fooling and ToM performance, outperforming Gemini3-Pro and GPT-5.4 with ToM prompting on hard scenarios. We also show that ToM-SB and AI Double Agents can be extended to stronger attackers, demonstrating generalization to OOD settings and the upgradability of our task.

item.title: Understanding and Accelerating the Training of Masked Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.13026v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models (ARMs) for language modeling. However, MDMs are known to learn substantially more slowly than ARMs, which may become problematic when scaling MDMs to larger models. Therefore, we ask the following question: how can we accelerate standard MDM training while maintaining its final performance? To this end, we first provide a detailed analysis of why MDM training is slow. We find that the main factor is the locality bias of language: the predictive information for a token is concentrated in nearby positions. We further investigate how this bias slows learning and suggest a simple yet effective remedy: bell-shaped time sampling as a training strategy. Notably, MDMs trained with our training recipe reach the same validation negative log-likelihood (NLL) up to $\sim4\times$ faster than standard training on One Billion Word Benchmark (LM1B). We also show faster improvements in generative perplexity, zero-shot perplexity, and downstream task performance on various benchmarks.

item.title: A Sovereign, Open-Source Foundation Model for German and English [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.09424v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Soofi S 30B-A3B, a sovereign, open-source Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) hybrid Mamba Transformer foundation model for German and English. Its hybrid design activates only 3B of 30B parameters per token and keeps the inference cache near-constant as context grows, giving it a decisive throughput advantage over dense models for long-context, high-concurrency deployment. Pretrained on roughly 27 trillion tokens with deliberately up-weighted German, Soofi S matches dense 14 to 27B models on aggregate English and German benchmarks while achieving the best code aggregates in both languages among 17 open base models, and outperforms every European sovereign baseline in our comparison, including ones far larger in active parameters. Among fully open models, Soofi S obtains the highest English and German evaluation scores, ahead of Olmo 3 32B and Apertus 70B. Soofi S was built end-to-end on the German Industrial AI Cloud, a sovereign HPC scale AI infrastructure operated by Deutsche Telekom in Munich. Soofi S will be released under highly permissive, open-access terms: weights, selected intermediate checkpoints, full per-source data accounting, hyperparameters, and training and evaluation code. Where source licenses permit, data-construction artifacts are released under permissive licenses; commercially licensed sources are documented with aggregate statistics and exact mixture accounting.
